BIO_FACTS: Water is polar, so its molecules form [hydrogen] bonds with each other: this gives cohesion, adhesion and a high specific heat capacity.
Cohesion between water molecules lets [transpiration] pull water up xylem as an unbroken column under tension.
DNA's two strands are [antiparallel]: one runs 5'→3', the other 3'→5'.
Complementary base pairing (A-T, C-G in DNA) is held together by [hydrogen] bonds, which is what lets DNA be copied.
The Miller-Urey experiment showed that [amino acids] can form from simple inorganic molecules with energy (sparks).
Prokaryotes have [70S] ribosomes, a nucleoid region and no membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotes have 80S in the cytoplasm.
Endosymbiosis explains why mitochondria and chloroplasts have a double membrane, their own circular [DNA] and 70S ribosomes.
Viruses are not cells: they have no [metabolism] of their own and can only replicate inside a host cell.
The [biological species concept] defines a species as a group that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring.
A [clade] is a common ancestor plus all of its descendants.
[Homologous] structures (like the pentadactyl limb) are evidence of a common ancestor.
In situ conservation protects species in their natural habitat; [ex situ] conservation protects them elsewhere, like seed banks and zoos.
Monosaccharides join by [condensation] reactions, releasing water; hydrolysis splits them again.
Phospholipids form bilayers because they are [amphipathic]: a hydrophilic phosphate head and hydrophobic tails.
A protein's [tertiary] structure is its 3D folding, held by ionic bonds, hydrogen bonds, disulfide bridges and hydrophobic interactions.
Heat and extreme pH can [denature] a protein by breaking the bonds that hold its shape.
[Facilitated diffusion] moves molecules down a gradient through channel or carrier proteins, with no ATP.
The sodium-potassium pump moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in per [ATP] used: active transport.
The nuclear membrane separates [transcription] from translation in eukaryotes.
Surface area to volume ratio [decreases] as a cell grows, which limits cell size.
Alveoli have a large surface area, one-cell-thick walls and a dense [capillary] network for fast diffusion.
Arteries have thick walls with elastic and muscle tissue to withstand and maintain high [pressure].
In the sliding filament model, [myosin] heads bind actin and use ATP to pull the filaments past each other.
A [habitat] is the place where an organism lives; adaptations are traits that suit it to that habitat.
The competitive exclusion principle: two species cannot share the same [niche] for long in the same place.
A [competitive] inhibitor binds the active site; a non-competitive one binds elsewhere and changes the active site's shape.
Enzymes lower the [activation energy] of a reaction without being used up.
Anaerobic respiration in humans makes [lactate]; in yeast it makes ethanol and CO₂.
Most ATP in aerobic respiration is made by [chemiosmosis]: protons flow through ATP synthase.
In the light-dependent reactions, [photolysis] splits water, releasing oxygen as a by-product.
In the Calvin cycle, the enzyme [RuBisCo] fixes CO₂ onto RuBP.
Steroid hormones are lipid-soluble, so they pass the membrane and bind [intracellular] receptors.
A nerve impulse is an [action potential]: depolarisation as Na⁺ flows in, then repolarisation as K⁺ flows out.
Myelination speeds up impulses by [saltatory] conduction, jumping between nodes of Ranvier.
The [cerebellum] coordinates skeletal muscle movement and balance.
[Antibodies] are made by plasma cells, which come from activated B lymphocytes.
Vaccines make [memory cells] so a second infection gets a faster, bigger response.
Population growth often follows a [sigmoid] curve: exponential growth, then a plateau at carrying capacity.
Only about [10]% of energy passes from one trophic level to the next; the rest is lost, mostly as heat.
DNA replication is [semi-conservative]: each new double helix keeps one original strand.
DNA polymerase III can only add nucleotides in the [5' to 3'] direction.
During translation, tRNA anticodons pair with mRNA [codons] at the ribosome.
A base substitution can change one amino acid, as in [sickle cell] anaemia (GAG → GTG).
Crossing over in prophase I and [random orientation] in metaphase I both make meiosis produce variation.
[Methylation] of DNA usually switches genes off: an epigenetic change.
Water moves from higher to [lower] water potential.
[Meiosis] halves the chromosome number so fertilisation can restore it.
A [test cross] with a homozygous recessive individual reveals an unknown genotype.
Blood glucose is controlled by [negative feedback]: insulin lowers it, glucagon raises it.
Natural selection needs [variation] that is heritable, overproduction of offspring and competition.
A [keystone] species has a much bigger effect on its ecosystem than its numbers suggest.
Melting ice lowers [albedo], so more heat is absorbed: a positive feedback loop.
PSY_TERMS: The study measures what it claims to, without confounding variables.
How well findings apply to real-life settings.
Getting consistent results when the study or measure is repeated.
Defining a variable so it can be measured (e.g. 'stress' = cortisol level).
Participants guess the aim and change their behaviour.
The researcher's expectations influence the results or their interpretation.
Every member of the target population has an equal chance of being picked.
Using whoever is available at the time.
Participants volunteer, e.g. by answering an advert.
The same participants take part in every condition.
The IV is a naturally occurring characteristic (like age or gender), so participants aren't randomly allocated.
Using several methods, researchers or sources to check credibility in qualitative research.
Participants agree after being told what the study involves.
Explaining the true aim afterwards, especially after deception.
Whether qualitative findings apply to other settings or people.
Participants don't know they are being observed.
A group interview of about 3-8 people discussing a topic.
ENGLISH_TIPS: Open with a thesis that answers the guiding question AND names the text's purpose and audience. One sentence, no retelling.
Use the chain technique → effect → purpose: 'The second-person address ("you") draws the reader in, which makes the call to donate feel personal.'
Spend the first 15 minutes annotating: text type, audience, purpose, tone, structure, then 3-4 techniques with quotes.
Analyse the visuals too: layout, colour, font, image framing, gaze and vectors count as techniques in non-literary texts.
Embed short quotes (2-6 words) in your own sentence instead of dropping in long ones.
Structure by idea, not by line order: each paragraph proves one part of your thesis.
HL: you write two essays in 2h15. Plan both briefly before writing so the second one isn't rushed.
Compare in EVERY paragraph: 'Whereas Author A..., Author B...' Don't write one half on each work.
Pick the question whose key word fits BOTH works well, then define that key word in your introduction.
Prepare 4-5 short quotes per work by heart, each tagged with 2-3 themes so they fit many questions.
Talk about choices: 'Morrison chooses a fragmented structure to...' shows awareness of the writer at work.
Context only when it explains meaning: a sentence of context, then back to the text.
Name your global issue as a specific claim, not a topic: not 'gender', but 'how media pressures women to conform to beauty ideals'.
Split roughly evenly: about 5 minutes on the literary extract, 5 on the non-literary one, linking both to the global issue.
Bring the extracts (max 40 lines each) and a plan of up to 10 bullet points, no full sentences.
1200-1500 words on one work or a body of work; the line of inquiry should be focused and arguable.
Cite secondary sources if you use them, but your own analysis has to be the backbone.
Swap 'shows' for precise verbs: conveys, evokes, undermines, foregrounds, juxtaposes, satirises.
Avoid 'I think' or 'in my opinion'; argue with evidence: 'This suggests...', 'Arguably...'.
End paragraphs by linking back to the question, not with a summary of the quote.
Conclusion: answer the question in one fresh sentence, then say what this reveals about the writer's purpose or the text's wider meaning.
Analysis and evaluation: say how effective a choice is, not just what it is ('The statistic is persuasive but cold...').
Focus and organisation: topic sentences that make claims, plus clear transitions between ideas.
Language: vary sentence length, keep a formal register, and use literary/linguistic terms accurately.
PSY_PRACTICALS: naturalistic or controlled, overt or covert, participant or non-participant
closed and open questions, at least 10 participants
true or quasi-experiment, at least 5 participants

PSY_CONCEPTS.Bias: Systematic distortion: in thinking (cognitive biases), in research (researcher, participant, sampling bias) or in theories.
PSY_CONCEPTS.Causality: Can we say X causes Y? Only experiments show cause and effect; correlations and observations can't.
PSY_CONCEPTS.Change: How behaviour, the brain and cultures change over time (development, neuroplasticity, acculturation, treatment).
PSY_CONCEPTS.Measurement: How psychologists measure things they can't see (memory, stress, attachment): operationalisation, validity, reliability.
PSY_CONCEPTS.Perspective: Biological, cognitive and sociocultural approaches see the same behaviour differently; so do cultures and individuals.
PSY_CONCEPTS.Responsibility: Ethics towards participants and society: consent, deception, debriefing, right to withdraw, how findings are used.

Health and well-being: the effect of social support on health
Learning and cognition: the role of emotion in memory
